newsitem.title: USA: Cohen backs Navy on woman fighter pilot.
newsitem.headline: Cohen backs Navy on woman fighter pilot.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Cohen said Tuesday he supported the Navy's decision to return to limited flight status a woman jet fighter pilot who was grounded two years ago.

"I am satisfied that they would not make such a recommendation unless they felt secure that her qualifications would allow her to do that," he told reporters of the move allowing Lt. Carey Lohrenz to resume flying land-based Navy aircraft only.

"We are not interested in putting people's lives in jeopardy and so political correctness should not be a standard. And I don't believe the Navy is looking at it from that perspective," Cohen added when asked if last month's step might have been taken because Lohrenz was a woman.

In a controversial move, Lohrenz was grounded in May 1995 from flying F-14 fighter jets aboard aircraft carriers only one month after receiving an outstanding fitness report. The Navy said it was worried about her landing techniques.

Lohrenz, one of the service's first female fighter pilots, charged discriminatory treatment by superiors and colleagues of Carrier Air Wing 11 based at Miramar Naval Air Station in California. A Navy Inspector General's investigation report released Tuesday said her problems with carrier landings were in large measure due to stress and that it found a "lack of documentation demonstrating poor performance" on her part.

"Although the evidence indicates that Lieutenant Lohrenz's performance may not have been suitable for a carrier environment, there is nothing in the record to suggest that she would not be competent to fly in a non-carrier environment," the report said.

It also suggested that part of the system for integrating female combat pilots into the Navy fighting force was bungled. In its zeal to be "gender neutral," it said, the Navy opened the way for some squadron commanders to justify their failure to make reasonable accommodations to help struggling aviators, who happened to be women, for fear such accommodations would show preferential treatment.

Supporters of Lohrenz said when she was returned to flight status on June 21 that the move was a victory for the pilot. "I think the Navy is trying to do the right thing and I'm satisfied this is the best they can do at this time," Susan Barnes, an attorney for Lohrenz, told the Washington Post.
